title: Signs Your Sprinkler System Wasn't Fully Winterized
meta_title: Signs Your Sprinklers Weren't Fully Winterized
meta_description: A blowout that misses part of the system can look complete at the time. Here are the signs that point to water still trapped somewhere in the lines.
lede: A winterization job can look finished and still leave water trapped somewhere in the system. Here's what to watch for.
excerpt: How to spot a sprinkler system that wasn't fully cleared of water before winter.

sections.heading: Water Sitting in a Valve Box
paragraphs: Valve boxes sit at low points in the system by design, which makes them one of the first places water pools if it wasn't fully removed. If you check a valve box in late fall or winter and find standing water rather than dry components, that's a sign the system wasn't completely cleared.

sections.heading: Unusually Soft or Wet Ground Near Buried Lines
paragraphs: If a section of yard along a known sprinkler line stays noticeably softer or wetter than the surrounding soil going into winter, that can point to water that's still in the pipe below rather than fully drained out.

sections.heading: Sounds or Pressure Left in the System
paragraphs: A fully winterized system should have no pressure or water movement left in it. Any hissing, gurgling, or pressure you notice at a valve or fitting after winterization was supposedly complete suggests water or air is still trapped somewhere it shouldn't be.

sections.heading: Why These Signs Matter Before It's Too Late
paragraphs: Catching a partial winterization before a hard freeze gives you a chance to have it corrected. Once the freeze hits, whatever water is still in the system is at risk, and by then the fix is a spring repair instead of a fall follow-up.

faqs.q: What does standing water in a valve box actually mean?
faqs.a: It usually means the blowout didn't fully clear that section of the system, since valve boxes sit at low points where remaining water tends to collect.

faqs.q: Can I check for these signs myself?
faqs.a: Yes, a visual check of valve boxes and the ground near known lines doesn't require special equipment. If anything looks off, it's worth having it looked at before a freeze.

faqs.q: Is it worse to find this before or after a freeze?
faqs.a: Much better before. Catching a partial winterization ahead of a freeze allows it to be corrected, rather than dealing with damage that's already happened.
